decisions.reason: The legacy 210-4302 link is unscoped, lacks persisted product-identity evidence, and the catalog does not cover the article's 2014 endpoint; the newly reviewed scoped candidate must replace it.

sourceEvidence.title: Premature Alternator Failure
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace alternator. OE Denso or quality remanufactured unit recommended. Check serpentine belt and tensioner at the same time as a worn belt accelerates alternator bearing wear.

decisions.reason: The unscoped WPCH-707V claim is absent for the Hellcat application, incomplete across the 6.4L years, and does not prove the metal-impeller construction recommended by the article.

sourceEvidence.title: HEMI Water Pump Premature Failure / Coolant Leak
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnose first: with the engine off, check the water-pump pulley/shaft for play (rock it) and spin for roughness/grinding; inspect the pump body for a dried, thick glycol deposit trail (sign of a failed shaft seal — replacement is required), as distinct from a harmless light stain at the weep hole. Listen for a growl, squeal, or "frog-croak" bearing noise from the front of the engine, and watch for slowly rising coolant temp or a coolant smell. The repair is replacement of the water pump (the pump is not serviceable). When replacing, many owners and shops recommend a metal-impeller aftermarket pump (e.g., Gates) instead of another OEM plastic-impeller Mopar unit to avoid a repeat failure. Replace the thermostat and any brittle gaskets/hoses at the same time, refill with the correct OAT coolant, and bleed the system. If the impeller shed plastic before replacement, flush the cooling system thoroughly and inspect the radiator/thermostat for debris. Torque the pump mounting bolts to ~18 ft-lb on HEMI applications (verify per year/engine). Caught early (seal weep / bearing noise, no overheating), it is a straightforward cooling repair; caught late (impeller failure + overheat), it risks downstream engine damage — hence prompt attention to bearing noise or coolant loss.

decisions.reason: The unscoped 210-1227 claim is catalog-confirmed only for the 3.6L application and is absent for the article's 5.7L application; this recall-first issue must not expose that retail link broadly.

sourceEvidence.title: Sudden alternator failure causing stall, electrical loss, and fire risk (Recalls 14V634 & 17V435)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: If your VIN is covered by recall 14V634 or 17V435, the repair is FREE at any Dodge/Chrysler dealer regardless of mileage or age -- check your VIN at nhtsa.gov/recalls or call Stellantis/Chrysler customer care at 1-800-853-1403 (reference campaign P60 or T36). Under 14V634 the dealer replaces the alternator outright; under 17V435 the dealer first inspects the alternator part number and replaces it only if it is one of the suspect units. Out of warranty and not covered by the recall (e.g. some 5.7L or higher-amp configurations), a standard alternator replacement runs about 2 hours of labor: budget roughly $300-$600 for a quality remanufactured or new unit and $150-$400 in labor, with full RepairPal shop estimates of about $800-$1,180 for the era. Owner-reported real-world bills span $500 to $1,290 (the high end including a battery the failing alternator damaged). Because a failing diode can dump unregulated voltage or overheat the battery, have the battery load-tested at the same time and address any flickering-light, ABS/ESC-warning, or burning-smell symptoms immediately rather than waiting -- a fully shorted alternator is a fire and stall hazard. Verify any aftermarket replacement is rated for your car's amperage (160/180/220A) and EHPS load.

decisions.reason: The legacy 210-1183 claim is unscoped and appears only in a subset of the catalog engines represented by the article, so it can be shown for an unsupported HEMI application.

sourceEvidence.title: Alternator/Charging System Failure
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace alternator with OEM or quality aftermarket unit. Have battery tested and replaced if damaged from undercharging. Check for excessive electrical draw from accessories. Consider higher-output alternator for vehicles with added electrical accessories.

decisions.reason: The unscoped TE-26 claim is catalog-confirmed only through 2003 while the article continues through 2011 and names multiple transmission families.

sourceEvidence.title: Transmission Overdrive Solenoid Failure (42RE/45RFE)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace the overdrive solenoid and governor pressure solenoid as a pair — they are accessed by dropping the transmission pan and valve body. Use Mopar ATF+4 (68218058AC) exclusively. For the 42RE, the solenoid pack is inexpensive ($40-$80) but labor is 2-3 hours. For the 45RFE/545RFE, replace the entire solenoid block assembly. Regular fluid changes every 30,000 miles help prevent recurrence.

decisions.reason: The unscoped 210-1226 claim appears only for the 3.6L catalog application and can be shown for the article's unsupported V8 applications.

sourceEvidence.title: Alternator Failure
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace alternator with OEM or quality aftermarket. Test battery condition as it may be damaged from undercharging. Consider higher-output alternator if aftermarket accessories installed.

decisions.reason: The unscoped WPCH-608V claim is catalog-confirmed only for 2016-2021, leaving the article's 2011-2015 years unsupported; newly reviewed earlier-year candidates must remain separately scoped.

sourceEvidence.title: Water Pump Failure (Pentastar V6)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace water pump when symptoms appear or preventatively during timing chain service. Replace thermostat at same time. Consider timing chain inspection if high mileage.

decisions.reason: The unscoped 20-1042 claim is not catalog-supported for the article's 2008-2010 years and lacks persisted direct-product identity evidence.

sourceEvidence.title: Power Steering Pump Whine and Failure
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Flush the power steering system and refill with Mopar power steering fluid (MS-5931 spec). If the pump is whining, it is already worn internally and should be replaced (Mopar 68059524AD or equivalent remanufactured unit). Replace the reservoir cap as a standard practice during any PS service. A power steering pump replacement runs $250-$500 installed.

decisions.component: Engine Timing Belt Kit with Water Pump
decisions.reason: The unscoped WP295K2A kit is catalog-confirmed only for 1998-2004, while the article starts in 1993 and spans multiple engine applications.

sourceEvidence.title: 3.2L/3.5L V6 Timing Belt Tensioner and Water Pump Failure
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace the timing belt, water pump, tensioner, and idler pulleys together as a kit every 60,000-100,000 miles, using metal (not plastic) pulleys. If the belt has already failed on a 1998+ engine, a compression/leak-down test is needed first — bent valves require cylinder head removal and valve work.

decisions.reason: The unscoped 235-1061 crankshaft-sensor claim is not catalog-supported for the article's 2001-2004 endpoint and cannot represent both camshaft and crankshaft sensor branches without variant scope.

sourceEvidence.title: Camshaft/Crankshaft Position Sensor Failure — Intermittent Stalling and No-Start
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace the failed camshaft and/or crankshaft position sensor and inspect the connector and wiring for heat damage; many shops replace both sensors together since they fail similarly. It is an inexpensive bolt-in repair once correctly diagnosed.

decisions.reason: The unscoped 210-4326 claim is missing catalog support for the article's 2020 endpoint and does not preserve engine-specific application evidence.

sourceEvidence.title: Alternator Failure
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Test alternator output voltage and amperage to confirm failure. Replace alternator with quality rebuilt or new unit. Inspect serpentine belt and replace if necessary. Check battery condition - failing battery can damage alternator.

decisions.reason: Although 54664 appears in the reviewed 2.4L years, the legacy claim has no machine-enforceable fitment or persisted exact-product identity; it must be reintroduced only through the guarded scoped path.

sourceEvidence.title: Head Gasket Failure
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace head gasket which requires cylinder head removal. Have head inspected for warping and resurfaced if necessary. Replace thermostat and housing simultaneously. Check for additional engine damage from overheating.

decisions.reason: The unscoped THRCH-0002 thermostat appears only for the 2.4L catalog application and can be shown for unsupported V6 applications in the same article.

sourceEvidence.title: Engine Overheating - Thermostat Housing Debris
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Flush cooling system thoroughly to remove debris from thermostat housing port. Replace thermostat and housing gasket. In severe cases, thermostat housing replacement needed. Use only Mopar OAT coolant. Change coolant every 50,000 miles.

decisions.component: Engine Timing Belt Tensioner Hydraulic Assembly
decisions.reason: The legacy BTC-003 claim is unscoped and lacks persisted exact-listing identity evidence; its SOHC and DOHC application proof must be carried through a reviewed scoped replacement.

sourceEvidence.title: Interference-engine timing belt / hydraulic tensioner failure
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace the timing belt, the hydraulic tensioner, and the water pump together at roughly 60,000-100,000 mile intervals (and by age on older cars). Inspect idler and cam/crank seals while apart. If a belt has already broken, a valve job or head replacement may be required.
